opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I feel strongly about this. One of the most important skills of the coming years will be the ability to tell a computer exactly what you want it to do, so that it does it for you. For decades, that ability was mostly limited to software engineers, because you had to learn fairly arcane syntax to do it. Now, with AI coding assistants and large language models, the barrier to getting a computer to do what you want has dropped dramatically.

What I'm seeing is that people in non-engineering roles who know a little bit of coding, and know how to use AI well, are just much more productive than people who don't. Think of a marketer who can write a small script to analyze campaign data, or a recruiter who can build a simple tool to screen and organize candidate information. A financial analyst who can automate a report that used to take a day. These aren't huge engineering projects. They're small things, but they add up to a big difference in what one person can get done.

Some people have said, "AI will write the code, so you don't need to learn to code anymore." I think that's some of the worst career advice out there. When AI makes coding easier, more people should learn to code, not fewer. Look at history: when we went from punch cards to keyboards, or from assembly to higher-level languages, coding got easier and many more people learned to do it. The same thing is happening now. You still need to understand enough to describe what you want precisely, check whether the output is correct, and debug it when it isn't. That understanding is what lets you steer the AI, rather than just hoping it gets things right.

I've seen this on teams I work with, too. When people across functions, not just the engineers, get comfortable with AI tools and some basic coding, the whole organization moves faster. They stop waiting in a queue for engineering resources to build every little thing, and they can prototype ideas themselves. So I'd encourage everyone, whatever their job title, to learn to code a little and to get really good at using AI. It's one of the highest-leverage things you can do for your career right now.

r001.rationale: The response discusses effective AI use as an important skill but does not compare it to knowing how to search the web.

r002.rationale: It says non-engineers who know some coding and use AI well are more productive, with examples tied to marketing, recruiting, and financial analysis.

r003.rationale: It says coding helps people tell computers exactly what they want and describe requests precisely enough to steer AI.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, I think the question of whether everyone should learn to code has been kind of a flip-flopping debate for a long time. And my view is that as AI makes coding easier, more people should learn to code, not fewer. That sounds counterintuitive to a lot of people, so let me explain why.

If you look at the history of computing, every time programming got easier, the number of programmers went up. When we went from punch cards to keyboards and terminals, some people thought programming would become less important. Instead, way more people started doing it. When we went from assembly to COBOL, there were actually people saying, now that we have COBOL, we don't need programmers anymore. And of course the opposite happened. So AI-assisted coding is the latest step in that same trend of lowering the barrier.

Now, the reason this matters for people in non-engineering roles is that the ability to tell a computer exactly what you want it to do is one of the deepest skills you can have. Almost everyone in a knowledge work job interacts with computers all day. And if you understand a little bit about how software works, even if you never become a professional engineer, you can get the computer to do far more for you. I've seen marketers, recruiters, investors, people in my own front office, write small pieces of code or use AI tools to automate things that used to take them hours. A marketer who can code can run their own analysis instead of waiting a week for an engineer to get to the ticket.

And there's a second piece, which is effective use of AI more broadly. A lot of people have tried ChatGPT or Claude or whatever once, asked a question, got a mediocre answer, and concluded it's not that useful. But using these tools well is actually a skill. Knowing what to ask, how to give context, when to trust the output and when to check it, how to break a task into pieces the model can handle. People who develop that skill are often dramatically more productive than their peers, and I think the gap between people who use AI well and people who don't will only get wider.

So my advice, honestly, is that everyone should learn at least a little bit of coding. Not because everyone will be a software engineer, but because in the same way that reading and writing used to be specialized skills and became universal, being able to make computers do what you want is becoming a basic literacy. And the tools are now so good that the time investment is lower than it's ever been.

r001.rationale: The response describes effective AI use as a skill, but does not compare it to knowing how to search the web.

r002.rationale: It says non-engineers such as marketers can automate work and run their own analysis, improving how they perform their existing jobs.

r003.rationale: It explicitly describes coding as the ability to tell a computer exactly what you want it to do.

astra-6.text:
I think AI is making it possible for many more people to build things. And that matters even if your job title isn’t software engineer. If you work in marketing, finance, or HR, you understand problems in your work that someone outside your field might never notice. Being able to use AI—and write a little code with its help—gives you a way to solve those problems yourself.

There’s a temptation to say, if AI can write code, why should I learn to code? But knowing the basics helps you tell the AI what you want, understand what it produces, and check whether it’s actually doing the right thing. You don’t have to become a professional developer to benefit from that.

For example, you might have a repetitive task involving a spreadsheet. You can ask an AI for advice, which is useful. But if you can work with it to build a small program that does the task, you’ve changed how you work. I think that ability to go from an idea to something that runs is becoming valuable across a lot of professions.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI and coding as useful workplace skills but makes no comparison to knowing how to search the web.

r002.rationale: It says coding with AI lets people solve problems in their own work and build programs for repetitive tasks, changing how they work across professions.

r003.rationale: It says coding basics help people tell AI what they want, which conveys using code to direct a computer toward a desired result.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of AI as a general-purpose technology. Its impact won’t be limited to software engineering. Marketing, finance, operations, HR—there are opportunities in all of these functions. And often, the person who understands the work is best positioned to see where AI can help. They know which tasks are repetitive, where the bottlenecks are, and what a useful result would look like.

Learning to code gives that person more ability to act on those ideas. You don’t have to become a professional software engineer. Even a little programming knowledge can help you connect tools, analyze data, or build a prototype. And with AI helping you write code, the amount you can accomplish with that knowledge is growing.

But you still need judgment. You need to specify what you want, check whether the output makes sense, and recognize when something has gone wrong. So I see effective AI use and coding as complementary skills. They give people more control over their work and let them solve problems that previously would have required waiting for someone else to build a solution.

r001.rationale: The response calls AI a general-purpose workplace technology but does not compare effective AI use to knowing how to search the web.

r002.rationale: It says coding helps people apply ideas in their own functions, connect tools, analyze data, and solve work problems, communicating improved ability to perform their existing work.

r003.rationale: It says effective AI use requires specifying desired results, but does not explain that learning to code lets people give computers more precise instructions.
